plain: Supabase is the storage where your application keeps what needs to still be there tomorrow: users, orders, messages, photos. Think of an office filing cabinet with its drawers and neatly organized records, except instead of sitting in your house it's on a computer running 24 hours a day that your website talks to from anywhere. It comes with sign-up and login already built (email, password, sign-in-with-Google button) and a lock on every single record, so each customer sees only their own and nothing else. You decide what gets stored and who can open each drawer; they provide the machine, the power, and the maintenance.

account.free: Yes, and the free tier is enough to actually build something: 2 active projects, 500 MB of database, 1 GB of files, 5 GB of monthly traffic, and up to 50,000 distinct monthly active users. Two catches with the free tier: if nobody touches the project for a week it pauses (you reactivate it with one click from the dashboard, nothing gets deleted), and there are no automatic backups. The Pro plan costs $25 a month per organization, roughly €23 depending on the day's exchange rate, and it's billed in dollars: it removes the pause, raises you to 8 GB of database, and keeps daily backups for the last 7 days. Supabase adjusts prices from time to time; check supabase.com/pricing before entering your card.
steps: On supabase.com click the green button top right, 'Start your project'. It offers signing in with GitHub or your email. If you don't know what GitHub is, choose email: it works exactly the same. It never asks for a card.

It asks for 'New organization'. It's just a label to group your projects and for billing: put your name or your business's name. Under 'Plan' leave 'Free' checked. Choose another one and billing starts that same day.

'New project' button. Three fields: 'Name' (e.g. customer-notes), 'Database Password', and 'Region' (the country where the machine will live). If your users are in Spain, choose 'Central EU (Frankfurt)' or 'West EU (Ireland)': the closer, the faster the response. It takes a couple of minutes to set up and you'll see a progress bar.

Click 'Generate a password' and paste it into your password manager right away, not in a bit. Once you close that screen it's never shown again. If you lose it you can set a new one in 'Project Settings' > 'Database', but everything already connected with the old one stops working until you update it.
Create your first table from the interface

Left menu, 'Table Editor', green 'New table' button. Name it in lowercase with no accents, e.g. notes. Under 'Columns' you'll already see id and created_at: don't touch them, they're the numbered record and the creation date. Add your own with '+ Add column', choosing the type: text for text, int8 for whole numbers, bool for yes/no, timestamptz for dates, uuid for a user's identifier. Below you'll see a checked box, 'Enable Row Level Security (RLS)'. Do NOT uncheck it, even though the site warns you that you won't see data this way. It's correct that you don't see it yet.
Save the two keys and know which one goes to the browser

Bottom of the left menu, 'Project Settings' > 'API Keys'. You'll see your project's URL and two keys. The public one appears as 'anon public', or on newer projects, as 'Publishable key' starting with sb_publishable_. That's the one that goes inside your website. The other appears as 'service_role secret' or 'Secret key' and starts with sb_secret_: don't copy that one yet. Supabase changed the names and both versions coexist, so look at the 'public' or 'secret' label, not the exact name.

With row-level security on, your table returns nothing to anyone until you write a rule. Go to 'Authentication' > 'Policies', pick your table, and click 'New Policy'. Supabase offers ready-made templates: the one you almost always want is 'Enable read access for users based on user_id' (let people read only their own). Check it: the condition should read auth.uid() = user_id. Save and test your application again.
account.warning: The 'service_role' key (or 'Secret key') skips every security rule you write, no exceptions, by design. Whoever has it can read, change, and delete everything belonging to all your users in seconds, and deleting rows in a database has no recycle bin: without a backup, they're gone forever. That key never goes into code that reaches the browser, or into a mobile app, or gets uploaded to GitHub, or pasted into a chat with anyone. If you suspect it's leaked, go to 'Project Settings' > 'API Keys' and generate a new one that same day.

first: Open 'Table Editor' and create a notes table with three columns of your own: titulo (text), contenido (text), and user_id (uuid), leaving 'Enable Row Level Security' checked.
Go to 'Authentication' > 'Users' > 'Add user' > 'Create new user' and create a test user with an email of yours and any password. Copy the long identifier from the 'UID' column.
Open 'Table Editor' > 'Insert' > 'Insert row' and add two notes by hand, pasting that identifier into user_id, so you have real data to test with.
Go to 'Authentication' > 'Policies', click 'New Policy', pick the read template, and check that the condition says auth.uid() = user_id.
Create a second test user, log in with it from your application, and check that it sees zero notes. That zero is the sign the lock is working.
shortcuts: Opens the dashboard's command search. Type 'notes' and jump to that table, or type 'api' and it takes you to the keys. Saves you wandering through the left menu fifty times a day. If it doesn't open anything, use the 'Search' magnifying glass at the top: the dashboard's shortcuts change from time to time.
Ctrl + Enter (Cmd + Enter on Mac) in the SQL Editor

Runs the query you've written. It's the move you'll repeat every time the AI gives you a piece of code: paste and Ctrl+Enter. With text selected, it runs only the selection, which is how you test one block out of three without firing all three.
Green 'Run' button, bottom right of the SQL Editor
Same thing with the mouse. Next to it you'll see how long it took and how many rows were affected. If it says 'Success. No rows returned', it ran fine and simply had nothing to return: not an error.

A blank sheet for pasting whatever the AI gives you. Save each one under its own named query ('create orders table', 'orders policies'): that way you have a history of everything you've done to the database, which is your only memory of what you touched on Tuesday.

Supabase's built-in AI chat, right inside the website. It sees your tables, so you can ask it 'write me the policy so each user sees only their own orders' and it hands it to you ready to run. Always read what it proposes before running it: it's the one writing, but pressing the button is your responsibility.

The list of your security issues, in red. The first thing that always shows up is 'RLS Disabled in Public': wide-open tables. Check it every time you create a table, and again the day before you publish. It's free and takes five seconds.
'Table Editor': the gray label next to the table name
Says 'RLS enabled' or 'RLS disabled'. It's the fastest check there is and the one most people skip. If it says disabled and that table has people's data, you're publishing their data.

Creates test users by hand, skipping the confirmation email. You need two: one to see their own stuff and another to check they can't see the first one's. Without two users you can't know if security actually works.

The record of everything your site has asked Supabase and what it answered. When something 'doesn't work and no error shows up', this is where you see if the request arrived and with what code: 401 (unauthorized), 404 (doesn't exist), 200 (went fine and returned empty). Each response tells a different story.
daily: Creating and editing tables from 'Table Editor' with the mouse, no writing needed. 'New table' button, '+ Add column', and to enter data by hand, 'Insert' > 'Insert row'. 80% of what you need at the start happens here.

Pasting the code the AI writes into 'SQL Editor' and hitting Ctrl+Enter. You don't need to understand all of it, but read it looking for two words: 'drop' and 'delete'. If they show up and you didn't ask to delete anything, stop and ask.

Checking the 'RLS enabled' / 'RLS disabled' label next to each table, and running the 'Security Advisor' before showing the site to anyone. Two five-second checks that prevent the most expensive mistake.
Copying the project URL and the public key from 'Project Settings' > 'API Keys' and pasting them into your site's configuration file. The secret key stays on Supabase's website, it never leaves.

Testing with two users. Create them in 'Authentication' > 'Users', log in with one, then the other, and check whether it sees something it shouldn't. It's the only security test you need to do, and it has to be redone every time you add a table.

Asking the AI for queries in plain language, pasting the columns exactly as they appear in the Table Editor. Without those columns it invents them, and then you get an error about a column that doesn't exist.

Opening the dashboard once a week even if you do nothing, if you're on the free plan. After 7 days of no activity the project pauses; it reactivates with one click from the dashboard, but while paused your site doesn't respond.

templates.name: A private table with the full lock (per-user notes)
templates.what: The basic structure of almost any application with users: a table where each person sees, creates, changes, and deletes only their own. Works the same for notes, orders, tasks, appointments, or messages: change the name and the columns and the rest holds as is. Includes what almost everyone forgets: the lock and the four rules.
templates.how: 1) Left menu > 'SQL Editor' > 'New query'. 2) Paste the whole block, first line to last. 3) Replace notes with your table's name on EVERY line (there's no Ctrl+F: do it by eye, there are 9 spots). 4) Ctrl+Enter. 5) It should say 'Success. No rows returned'. 6) Go to 'Table Editor' and check that it says 'RLS enabled' next to the name.
fill: Your table's name, lowercase, no accents, no special characters, no spaces
Your real columns: customer_name, amount, phone, whatever you're storing
Each column's type: text for text, int8 for whole numbers, numeric for money, bool for yes/no, timestamptz for dates

templates.name: A public form nobody can read (waitlist)
templates.what: For landing pages, waitlists, contact forms, and reservations: anyone visiting your site can sign up, but nobody can read the list from outside. You can see it, from the 'Table Editor', because the dashboard comes in through a different door. It's the case people get wrong most often: they leave the table open for reading and anyone can download the emails of every interested person.
templates.how: 1) 'SQL Editor' > 'New query'. 2) Paste the whole block and hit Ctrl+Enter. 3) Test from your site by signing up an email: it should save. 4) Test reading the table from your site: it should return an empty list. Both together mean it's set up correctly. 5) See the actual list in 'Table Editor' > waitlist.
fill: Your table's name: contacts, reservations, quotes...
Your form's fields, one per column
Remove it if you want to allow the same email to sign up twice
templates.code:
create table public.waitlist (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  email text not null unique,
  name text,
  source text,
  created_at timestamptz not null default now()
);

alter table public.waitlist enable row level security;

-- Anyone visiting the site can sign up, logged in or not.
create policy "anyone can sign up"
  on public.waitlist for insert
  to anon, authenticated
  with check ( true );

-- And nobody can read it, change it, or delete it from the website:
-- since there's no select, update, or delete policy,
-- those three actions are closed off to everyone.
-- You see the list from the dashboard's Table Editor, which doesn't go through here.

templates.name: Connecting from your site: the .env file and the client
templates.what: The two files that connect your page to Supabase, with the public key kept out of the code. Works for any site built with React, Next.js, Vite, Lovable, Bolt, or v0. It's the template that prevents the classic accident: pasting the secret key here because 'the other one wasn't working'.
templates.how: 1) Copy the URL and the public key from 'Project Settings' > 'API Keys'. 2) Create a file called .env.local in your project's main folder and paste in the first block. 3) Create src/supabase.js with the second block. 4) Add the .env.local line to your .gitignore, if you have one: that's what stops the key from ending up on the internet. 5) Restart your site's server: .env files are only read on startup.
fill: The key labeled 'anon public' or 'Publishable key'. Never the 'secret' one
Your table, and in the select whatever columns you want to show
If your project is Next.js, change VITE_ to NEXT_PUBLIC_ in both files

templates.name: Audit cheat sheet: which tables are wide open
templates.what: A five-line query that tells you, at a glance, which of your tables are protected and which are open to anyone who has your public key. Run it before showing the site to anyone and every time the AI has created tables for you.
templates.how: 1) 'SQL Editor' > 'New query'. 2) Paste and hit Ctrl+Enter. 3) Read the 'status' column. 4) Any table marked OPEN TO ANYONE that has people's data is fixed with: alter table public.NAME enable row level security; and then its policies. 5) Save the query as 'audit' to repeat it in one click.
fill: Leave it as is unless you've created tables somewhere else, which you won't have
templates.code:
select
  tablename as table_name,
  case when rowsecurity
       then 'protected'
       else 'OPEN TO ANYONE'
  end as status
from pg_tables
where schemaname = 'public'
order by rowsecurity asc, tablename;

errors: new row violates row-level security policy for table "notes"

Translation: 'the new row breaks the notes table's rule'. You tried to save something and the lock stopped it. Three causes, most to least frequent: no insert policy exists (you only created the read one); the policy exists but your code isn't filling user_id with the user's identifier; or the user isn't logged in and to Supabase they're a stranger. Fix: create the insert policy with with check ( auth.uid() = user_id ) and make sure you're saving user_id.
The list comes back empty, no red error. It used to show 47 rows.

Supabase's most confusing symptom, and it's not broken: without a read policy, the correct behavior is to return nothing. The query ran fine, simply no row passed the filter, so there's no error to show. Usual culprits: there's no select policy, or there is one but your site is querying without a logged-in session, so auth.uid() is empty and doesn't match any user_id. Never fix it by turning security off.
Could not find the table 'public.notes' in the schema cache

'Can't find the notes table.' Almost always it's the name: you wrote it as Notes with a capital and you're requesting notes, or you added an accent, or the AI made up the name. Check it in 'Table Editor' and copy it exactly. If the name is correct and you just created it, Supabase takes a few seconds to catch up: wait and reload. If it persists, go to 'Project Settings' > 'API' and check that the public schema is in 'Exposed schemas'.
Could not find the 'title' column of 'notes' in the schema cache

The same thing but with a column. The column your code is trying to write doesn't exist under that name: almost always an accent, a capital letter, or a name the AI guessed. Open the table in 'Table Editor', copy the exact header names, and give them to the AI asking it to fix the code with those names.

'Invalid key.' Three causes: you copied the key only halfway (they're very long, use the copy icon, not the mouse); a space or line break slipped in when pasting it into the .env file; or you put in the key from a different project. Go back to 'Project Settings' > 'API Keys', click the public key's copy icon, paste it cleanly, and restart your site's server: .env files are only read on startup.
null value in column "user_id" of relation "notes" violates not-null constraint

'The user_id column can't be left empty, and you left it empty.' Your form saves the title and content but doesn't say whose note it is. Two fixes: have the code include user_id when saving, or better, set the column's default value to auth.uid() with this line in the SQL Editor: alter table public.notes alter column user_id set default auth.uid(); That way it fills itself in automatically with whoever's logged in.
infinite recursion detected in policy for relation "profiles"

'The rule bites its own tail.' You've written a policy on the profiles table that, to decide whether it lets you view profiles, queries the profiles table itself. The database loops and cuts it off. Always happens when setting up admin roles. Fixed by pulling the value from the session instead of the table, or wrapping it in a function marked security definer. Paste the error and your policy to the AI and ask for exactly that.
For security purposes, you can only request this after 60 seconds / Email rate limit exceeded

'You've requested too many emails in a row.' The free email service Supabase gives you for testing sends very few messages per hour on purpose, and testing sign-up with your own email exhausts it in five minutes. To test, create users by hand in 'Authentication' > 'Users' > 'Add user', which skips the email. When you actually publish you'll need to connect your own sending service in 'Authentication' > 'Emails' > 'SMTP Settings'.

prompts.name: Have the AI design your tables from your idea
prompts.prompt: Act as the database architect for my Supabase project. I don't know how to code and I'm going to copy and paste whatever you give me into the SQL Editor, so I need complete code, not fragments. My idea is: [DESCRIBE YOUR PROJECT IN THREE SENTENCES, E.G.: A WEBSITE WHERE PHOTOGRAPHERS UPLOAD PHOTOS AND CLIENTS BUY THEM]. The types of people who will use it are: [E.G.: PHOTOGRAPHER, CLIENT, ADMIN]. The things I think I need to store are: [LIST WHATEVER COMES TO MIND, NO ORDER OR CRITERIA]. Before writing anything, ask me up to five questions to clarify anything unclear, one at a time, in plain language with no untranslated jargon. Once I've answered, give me in this order: (1) the list of tables with their columns, each one's type, and why it's there, explained as if to my mother; (2) a text diagram of how they relate to each other; (3) the complete SQL ready to paste, including alter table ... enable row level security on EVERY table and the corresponding policies; (4) a final list of the debatable decisions you've made for me. Rules: whenever a piece of data belongs to a person, always use a user_id column of type uuid referencing auth.users with on delete cascade. Name tables and columns in lowercase, no accents, no special characters, no spaces. Don't give me three options to choose from: pick the simplest and tell me at the end what you ruled out and why.

prompts.name: Have the AI write your security rules and explain them
prompts.prompt: You're my Supabase security expert and I don't know how to code. I have a table called [TABLE NAME] with these columns: [PASTE THE COLUMNS EXACTLY AS SHOWN IN THE TABLE EDITOR, WITH THEIR TYPES]. I want the rules to work like this, in plain terms: [DESCRIBE WHO CAN DO WHAT, E.G.: EACH USER SEES AND EDITS ONLY THEIR OWN ORDERS, ADMINS SEE ALL OF THEM, ANYONE CAN SIGN UP BUT NOBODY CAN READ THE LIST]. Write me the complete SQL, ready to paste into the SQL Editor, with this structure: first the alter table that turns on row-level security; then a separate policy for each action (select, insert, update, delete), each with a name explaining what it does; and in the insert and update ones, don't forget with check alongside using. Above each block write a two-dash comment explaining in one sentence what that rule allows. After the code, give me a two-column table: what a stranger sees and can do, and what the data's owner sees and can do, action by action. Also explain how I check this myself by creating two test users in Authentication > Users, with the exact clicks. And warn me if any rule I've asked for leaves something open that I haven't noticed. Don't use using (true) in any read policy unless I've told you that data is intentionally public; if you do use it, write it in capital letters so I notice.

prompts.name: Have the AI write the query that talks to your database
prompts.prompt: I need the code that talks to Supabase from my site and I don't code: I only copy, paste, and test. My project is built with [SAY WHAT YOU USE: PLAIN HTML, REACT, NEXT.JS, VITE, LOVABLE, BOLT, V0, OR 'I DON'T KNOW']. The table is called [NAME] and has these exact columns: [PASTE THEM COPIED FROM THE TABLE EDITOR]. What I want the screen to do is: [DESCRIBE THE ACTION, E.G.: SHOW MY ORDERS FROM NEWEST TO OLDEST, WITH A SEARCH BY CUSTOMER NAME AND A BUTTON TO CREATE A NEW ONE]. Requirements you can't skip: use the @supabase/supabase-js library; the URL and key are read from environment variables, never written inside the code; never use the service_role key in a file that reaches the browser; always check the error Supabase returns and show it on screen translated into a plain-language message a normal person understands, not the raw English text. Give me the complete file, all of it, no ellipses or 'rest goes here', because I don't know how to fill in gaps. Put a comment above each block saying what it does. At the end, separately and as a list: which files I create, where I save them, what I write in the .env file, and how I check in the browser that it works. If my query can return an empty list because of the security policies, tell me and explain what to check before assuming the code is broken.

prompts.name: Have the AI translate an error and give you the fix
prompts.prompt: I got this error while working with Supabase and I don't know what it means: [PASTE THE COMPLETE MESSAGE, EXACTLY AS IS, WITHOUT REMOVING OR TRANSLATING ANYTHING]. Context: the table involved is [NAME], I was trying to [WHAT YOU WERE DOING: SAVE, READ, DELETE, REGISTER A USER], and the error appears [WHERE: ON MY SITE'S SCREEN, IN THE BROWSER CONSOLE, IN SUPABASE'S SQL EDITOR]. This is the code that triggers it: [PASTE THE SNIPPET]. And these are the security policies I currently have set on that table: [PASTE THEM, OR WRITE 'I DON'T KNOW HOW TO SEE THEM' AND THEN EXPLAIN FIRST HOW TO PULL THEM UP]. Answer me in this order and don't skip anything: (1) what the error means in a single sentence, without a single untranslated technical word in parentheses; (2) the three most likely causes, ranked from most to least likely, with the specific sign that tells one apart from another; (3) how I check which one it is, with exact clicks in the Supabase dashboard or queries I can paste into the SQL Editor; (4) the fix, in complete code ready to copy; (5) how I confirm it's really fixed and not just stopped failing. If the fix you come up with is turning off row-level security, don't propose it: give me the alternative that keeps the lock on. And if any step deletes data or is irreversible, write it in capital letters right before the code.

prompts.name: Have the AI do a security audit before publishing
prompts.prompt: I'm about to publish my project and I want a security review of my Supabase database before anyone sees it. Act as a skeptical auditor, not a cheerleader: if something's wrong, say so clearly and first. These are my tables with their columns: [PASTE THEM, OR ASK ME TO RUN A QUERY IN THE SQL EDITOR TO GET YOU THE LIST AND GIVE IT TO YOU]. These are the security policies I have: [PASTE THEM]. My project is [DESCRIBE IT IN TWO SENTENCES] and the most sensitive data I store is [E.G.: EMAILS, PHONE NUMBERS, ADDRESSES, AMOUNTS, PRIVATE MESSAGES]. I want you to give me: (1) the list of tables that don't have row-level security enabled, with the SQL to enable it on each one; (2) the policies that let more through than I think, each with a concrete example of what a stranger who has my public key could do, which is anyone who opens my site and presses F12; (3) the columns that shouldn't be there, like passwords stored in plain text or card data; (4) exactly what happens if someone calls my database without being logged in, table by table; (5) a final ten-point checklist, in plain language, that I can go through on my own every time I add a new table. Order it all by severity, starting with what could ruin me. Don't run anything yourself: tell me what to run and warn me about anything irreversible.

words: Database

The storage where your application keeps what needs to still be there tomorrow: users, orders, messages. It's similar to a spreadsheet, but built for thousands of people to write at once without stepping on each other.
Table
A list of things of the same type, with the same fields for all of them. The customers table has name, email, and phone in every row. Just like a spreadsheet with headers at the top.
Row and column

The row is a specific line: one customer, one note, one order. The column is one of the fields every row has: the email, the amount. When someone says 'a record was created', they mean a row was added.
Row Level Security (RLS)

Row-based security. Rules that say, row by row, who can see it and who can't. Without it, permission is all-or-nothing. With it, Ana sees her own three notes and none of Javier's. Turned on with a checkbox when creating the table, or with one line if the AI created the table via SQL.
Policy

Each of those rules, written as a condition: 'this row can be read by whoever is logged in and owns it'. You write one per action: one for viewing (select), one for adding (insert), one for changing (update), and one for deleting (delete).
Anon / publishable key

A long code your site shows to identify itself to Supabase. It's public on purpose: it travels inside the page and anyone can see it by right-clicking and 'Inspect'. Nothing wrong with it being visible, as long as the policies are in place. It's not a lock, it's a doorbell.
Service_role / secret key
The total-control code. Ignores every rule you've written and gets into everything. Its place is a server of yours the visitor can't see, never the page that opens on your customer's phone.
SQL

The language used to talk to the database: 'give me the notes rows for user X'. You don't need to learn it. You do need to recognize two words when the AI gives you code: drop (destroy an entire table) and delete (remove rows). Both are irreversible.
auth.uid()

A shortcut meaning 'the identifier of the person currently using the application'. It's the centerpiece of almost every policy: auth.uid() = user_id translates to 'this row is yours'. If nobody is logged in, it's empty and matches nothing, which is exactly what you want.
Public schema

The default drawer where your tables live, and the only one your site can reach out of the box. That's why the code says public.notes. If a table ends up in another drawer, your application can't find it and you get a table-doesn't-exist error.
matters: Without row-level security enabled, your database is public even if you don't know it and even if your application works perfectly. Any visitor opens your site, presses F12, finds the public key in two minutes, and asks Supabase for the entire customers table with emails and phone numbers. It's not a sophisticated attack: it's copy and paste. It's Supabase's number one mistake, by far, and it's happened to companies with millions in funding.

Tables created by writing SQL do NOT have the lock on. The checkbox that's checked by default only exists in the visual table editor. If the AI dictates create table orders (...) and you paste it into the SQL Editor, that table is born wide open and nobody warns you of anything. After creating it, always run: alter table public.orders enable row level security; and then its policies.

The secret key doesn't belong in the browser. The moment you paste it into your site's code, it downloads with the page onto every visitor's computer. Whoever reads it doesn't just see your data: they can empty entire tables. Deleting rows is instant and has no recycle bin, and on the free plan there's no automatic backup to rescue anything. If you think it's leaked, regenerate it today.

When you turn the lock on and your application returns an empty list, it's not broken: it's doing exactly what it should. The default behavior is to deny everything until you write a rule that allows something, and it doesn't error because technically the query ran fine. Add the policies one at a time and test after each one, with two different users. And never fix it by turning off security 'just for the demo': that demo ends up being the published site.
ignore: Edge Functions (pieces of your own code that run on Supabase's servers). Useful the day you need to charge a card or call another service secretly. That day will come; not today.

Realtime, the feature that makes the screen update itself when another user changes something, Google-Docs style. Flashy, and turned on with a switch, but it complicates finding bugs while you're still wrestling with the basics.

The 'Database' > 'Extensions' tab, with over fifty add-ons for maps, search, and task queues. Off by default, and that's fine. You'll come back to that list the day you want to search by meaning using AI: the add-on is called pgvector.

questions.prompt: You've built a notes application and it works: you save notes, read them, all good. You created the table by writing create table notes (...) in the SQL Editor because an AI dictated it to you. You publish the site and show it to a friend. He presses F12, sees the anon key in the code, pastes it into a tool, and within thirty seconds is reading every registered user's notes, including yours. What went wrong?

options.text: The table was created via SQL and was born without row-level security. You need to run alter table notes enable row level security; and then create the policy that limits each note to its owner.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance matters: the checkbox that turns on security only appears in the visual table editor. When you create the table via SQL, nobody warns you it's open, and since your application works perfectly, you have no signal anything's wrong. The anon key did exactly its job: identify itself. The problem is there was no rule telling it which rows it can see.

options.text: Your anon key has leaked. You need to generate a new one from the settings and never leave it in the site's code again.
options.why: It's genuinely believable because it sounds like a classic leak: a secret code ends up visible and gets changed. But the anon key is designed to go in the browser, there's no way for your site to work without showing it. It breaks right there: you generate a new one, your friend presses F12 again, and sees it just as fast. The hole isn't the key, it's that nobody wrote the rules.

options.text: You should have used the service_role key in the application, since it's the admin key and controls who gets in better.
options.why: It's believable because in almost every program the admin account is the most protected, and the name sounds serious. It breaks in the worst possible way: that key ignores every rule and grants total control. Putting it in the site turns a 'they can read the notes' problem into 'anyone can delete the entire database', with no recycle bin and no backup on the free plan.

questions.explain: The anon key isn't the lock, it's the doorbell. The lock is the row-level rules, and tables created via SQL are born without them.

questions.prompt: You enable row-level security on the customers table. You reload your application and the list comes back empty: zero customers, no red error message, just empty. It used to show 47. You have a demo with a real client in two hours. What do you do?

options.text: Nothing is broken: without written policies, the correct behavior is to return nothing. You create a read policy with the condition auth.uid() = user_id and check that your application is sending the logged-in user's session.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is that an error-free empty result is this problem's signature, not a coincidence. Supabase doesn't return a failure because technically the query ran fine: simply no row passed the filter. The two usual culprits are that there's no policy, or there is one but your application is querying without a logged-in session, so auth.uid() is empty and matches no user_id.

options.text: You turn off row-level security so the demo goes well and turn it back on before actually publishing.
options.why: It's believable because it's true: it works in ten seconds, the demo goes well, and it sounds reasonable as something temporary. It breaks on the word 'afterward'. The demo goes well, the client asks for a URL to show their team, you give it to them, and that URL is now public with the table wide open. This is literally the most repeated security mistake in Supabase projects, and it almost always started as a two-hour patch.

options.text: You swap the anon key for the service_role one in the code, since that one does see the 47 customers.
options.why: It's believable because it works instantly and confirms 'the data is still there', which is very reassuring when you're in a rush. It breaks in the reason it works: it sees the 47 because it skips security entirely. And if that code reaches the browser, you've just handed total control of your database to anyone who opens the page.

questions.explain: An empty list after enabling security is the good news: it means the rule is now in charge, not chance. Write the rule.
